When scoring a video script or directing a voice actor, the literature provides several concrete vocal exercises, script-marking notation rules, and line-level delivery examples:

---

### 1. Script-Marking Notation & Scoring Rules
Before recording, the performance guidebooks recommend marking up copy in **pencil** using specific visual symbols to guide performance dynamics [1-3]:

* **Pitch Arrows (\\(\uparrow\\) / \\(\downarrow\\))**: Draw an **up arrow (\\(\uparrow\\))** above accent syllables requiring a pitch lift (questions, reveals, surprise, or sentence-opening attention-grabbers) and a **down arrow (\\(\downarrow\\))** for pitch drops (threats, commands, gravity, or punchlines) [1].
* **Hitting Words via Pitch (Not Volume)**: "Hitting" or "punching" a word means raising the pitch on its **accented syllable** (e.g., *EL-ephant* vs. *rhi-NOC-eros*), while keeping volume and emotional tone perfectly stable [158, 164–166]. Raising volume instead of pitch makes the delivery sound unnatural or aggressive [4, 5].
* **The "Pivot" (Siren Glide for Adjacent Key Words)**: When two important words appear side-by-side, shouting both destroys their impact [173–174]. Instead, use a "pivot"—glide pitch high on the first word's accent syllable, drop low in the middle, and sweep back up on the second word (modeled after *"Heeeeeeeeeeere's Johhhhhhhny!"*) [174–175].
* **Breath & Linkage Marks**: Annotate planned breath points, but also mark **places NOT to pause** (e.g., connecting words that start with vowels to avoid "glottal stops" or choppy hesitation) [2, 6, 7].

---

### 2. Line-Level Delivery Examples & Direction Tweaks

* **Hitting the First Word to "Open Up" the Read**:
  * *Direction*: Always hit one of the first words of a phrase or sentence to grab listener attention [8, 9].
  * *Example*: *"**WELCOME** to our company video"* or *"**BENEFIT** from our experience..."* [8, 10].
* **Focusing on the Positive Solution, Not the Negative Problem**:
  * *Direction*: In commercial or explainer scripts, hit the verb representing the positive solution rather than the negative condition you want to avoid [11].
  * *Example*: Read *"**PREVENT** drains from clogging"* by pitching up on *PREVENT*, rather than emphasizing *clogging* (which highlights the negative problem and creates a choppy pause) [11].
* **Pre-Sentencing with Lead-In Phrases**:
  * *Direction*: To hit the exact emotion on the very first word without a "warm-up lag," have the narrator silently or aloud speak a "lead-in" phrase right before starting the line [209–210].
  * *Example Script*: *"I was walking into my bank..."*
  * *With Lead-In*: *"[It was amazing,] I was walking into my bank..."* [209–210].
* **Conversational Contractions vs. Formal Clarity**:
  * *Informal Read*: Convert written text into natural conversational spoken forms: Read *"At Toyota, you will love what we are all about"* as *"At Toyota, you'll love what we're all about"* or *"Ya' know when it's hot..."* [12, 13].
  * *Formal Read*: Enunciate full words and hard consonants without contractions (e.g., pronouncing the "t" in *commitment*, *St. Vincent*, or *mountain*) [14, 15].
* **Digit Sequences & List Chunking**:
  * *Direction*: For multi-digit numbers, phone numbers, or automated menu prompts, alternate inflections across 3-part groups [192–193].
  * *Pattern*: Set digit 1 to **upward inflection**, digit 2 to **straight inflection**, and digit 3 to **downward inflection** (e.g., *"1 \\(\uparrow\\) – 2 \\(\rightarrow\\) – 3 \\(\downarrow\\)"*) to sound natural and prevent repetitive monotony [16].

---

### 3. Concrete Vocal Exercises & Drills

* **The 6-Step Pre-Talk Warm-Up Sequence** (Julian Treasure) [68–69]:
  1. **Breathing & Sighing**: Raise arms, inhale deeply, and exhale with an vocalized sigh (*"ahhhhh"*) [17].
  2. **Lip Activation**: Repeat *"Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba"* [17].
  3. **Lip Trill**: Vibrating lip buzz (*"Brrrrrrrrrr"*) [17].
  4. **Tongue Agility**: Exaggerated *"la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la"* [17].
  5. **Tongue Roll**: Rolling an R (*"Rrrrrrrrrr"*) [17].
  6. **Vocal Siren**: Sliding pitch continuously from high *"weee"* to low *"awww"* (*"weeeaawww"*) [17].
* **Air-Control & Stamina Drill**: Inhale deeply, hold air for 5 seconds, and exhale slowly while reciting the alphabet. Perform regularly to increase how many words can be spoken cleanly on a single breath without gasping [18].
* **"Lazy Mouth" Elimination Drill**: To stop unwanted "mmm" or "nnn" sounds before hard consonants (e.g., saying *"mmm-bye"* or *"nnn-Duracell"*), deliberately exaggerate the lazy mouth sound, notice mouth/tongue position, and incrementally reduce it down to zero [188–189].

3. When reading scripts written without enough punctuation marks, you’ll notice a tendency to run out of air. Therefore, adding punctuation marks is often necessary (see “punctuation” below). There are two exercises that can teach the body to have greater control of the intake and release of air, allowing longer periods of reading without running out of air. By employing them, recording sessions will go smoother, and the engineer will have fewer edits.   • any cardiovascular exercise  • air-controlling exercise: Inhale deeply, hold the air in for five seconds, and   then let it out slowly while saying the alphabet. By doing this regularly, you     will increase how many letters of the alphabet you can say on a single breath.
